prose_changes.old: Whether Lollardy fed directly into the English Reformation is still argued over by historians. What is not in doubt is that Lollard communities in the Chilterns, Essex, Coventry and Kent were still being prosecuted in the 1520s, exactly where and when the first English evangelicals appear, and that some of the same families turn up in both sets of records. Its most concrete survival is physical: around two hundred and fifty manuscripts of the Wycliffite Bible still exist, more than of any other Middle English text. A strange sort of monument for a movement its opponents believed they had stamped out.
prose_changes.new: Historians still argue over whether Lollardy fed straight into the English Reformation. What is not in doubt is that Lollard households were still on trial in the 1520s. In 1521 the bishop of Lincoln questioned many around Amersham in Buckinghamshire. Some had learned from Wyclif's Wicket, a short English tract on the sacrament. The Protestant writer John Foxe said this was before Luther's name was heard there. The movement's most solid survival is its books. Around two hundred and fifty handwritten copies of the Wycliffite Bible still exist, more than of any other Middle English text. It is a strange sort of monument for a movement its enemies thought they had stamped out.
